name: Sinaugoro
confidence_why: Tauberschmidt's 1999 reference grammar of the Saroa dialect places stress on the first syllable of words of one to three syllables and adds a weaker penultimate stress from four syllables up, with worked examples, and the only dissent is a one-sentence note in Kolia's 1975 sketch of the Balawaia dialect putting stress on the penult of words longer than two syllables, an older and thinner source on a different dialect that agrees with the grammar on disyllables and on a penult stress in longer words.
catalog_quote: 1.2.1.4.1 Stress and pitch on words. On one- to three-syllable words stress and high pitch is on the first syllable. ... On words with four syllables the first and penultimate syllable is stressed. However, the stress on the first syllable is stronger. ... 1.2.1.4.2 Stress and pitch on words in a phrase. Stress and high pitch of an isolated word can change when it occurs in a phrase: ['ka.ra da.'…

new_statements.quote: Stress is unmarked but always occurs on the first syllable of bisyllabic words and on the second last syllable of words of more than two syllables, e.g. 'ɡoɡo many, go'ɡome yam (sp.), 'ɡoɡolelevagi very many.
new_statements.citation: [NOT in the 'works' list; already held by the project from the 2026-09-16 pass] Kolia, J. A. 1975. A Balawaia grammar sketch and vocabulary. In T. E. Dutton (ed.), Studies in Languages of Central and South-East Papua (Pacific Linguistics C-29), 107-226.
new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened, p.3 = printed p.109 (rendered and read on the page scan). §1.21 Orthography reads: 'Stress is unmarked but always occurs on the first syllable of bisyllabic words and on the second last syllable of words of more than two syllables, e.g. 'gogo many, go'gome yam (sp.), 'gogolelevagi very many.' Verbatim apart from the glyph: the print uses a hooked-g letter for the velar fricative where the compiler wrote ɡ. The third example does carry an initial mark on the page ('gogolelevagi), as the compiler noted. Reading fixed: penultimate syllable is right (first syllable of a disyllable is its penult; all longer words penult). Relation 'contradicts' is right: the catalog string stress placeme…
new_statements.relation_note: Catalog (StressTyp2) gives stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 10010 100010 (1 = a stressed syllable), i.e. primary stress on the initial syllable with a second mark on the penult from four syllables up. Kolia puts the (only) stress on the penult: for disyllables both agree (initial = penult), but for trisyllables the catalog has 100 and Kolia predicts 010, and for longer words the catalog's primary is initial while Kolia's is penultimate. Kolia describes only the Balawaia dialect.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Balawaia dialect (Tauruba village): stress on the first syllable of disyllables and on the penult of longer words, i.e. penultimate stress throughout (the first syllable of a disyllable is its penult). No secondary stress mentioned. (In the print the examples use Kolia's hooked-g glyph for the voiced velar fricative, rendered ɡ here.)
new_statements.exceptions: Kolia's own third example, 'ɡoɡolelevagi 'very many', is marked with initial stress although the stated rule predicts penult for a six-syllable word; the word looks like a compound of ɡoɡo 'many' plus lelevagi, so the mark may be the stress of the first element or a slip. No other exceptions stated.
new_statements.identity_note: Kolia 1975 describes the Balawaia dialect of Sinaugoro as spoken in Tauruba village (Rigo sub-district); the Tauberschmidt dictionary and the StressTyp2 record do not name a dialect in the material opened. Dutton 1970 spells the language 'Sinagoro'.

readall_conflicts: The catalog's single record (StressTyp2: stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 10010 (1 = a stressed syllable), primary stress initial, a further mark on the penult from four syllables up) is contradicted by the only explicit statement opened, Kolia 1975 p. 109 on the Balawaia dialect, which puts stress on the first syllable of disyllables and on the penult of all longer words (i.e. penultimate stress). The two agree on disyllables and on a penult stress in 4+-syllable words, but disagree on trisyllables (initial vs penult) and on which syllable is primary in longer words. The listed work, Tauberschmidt's dictionary, is silent in its open (2007) form. The StressTyp2 record presumably rests on Tauberschmidt's 1999 grammar (PL C-143), which is not in the works list and could not be downloaded (sealang.net mirror: connection refused, then certificate failure; two attempts); the conflict cannot be settled from what was opened.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-strict, word domain, stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 10010 (1 = a stressed syllable): primary initial, secondary penult from four syllables up) rests on the standard reference grammar, Tauberschmidt 1999 PL C-143, which we hold as an open PDF with text; the deciding passage was confirmed verbatim at pp.10-11, including five-syllable verb words showing the 10010 shape. Glottolog 5.1 lists only two descriptive works; the full local Glottolog bib (18 entries) has no phonology article, OPD, JIPA piece or dissertation, and Dutton 1970:883 (downloaded) confirms nothing on Sinagoro phonology predates these. The one refinement found: Kolia 1975:109 (downloaded, open PL C-29) gives the Balawaia dialect penultimate stress in words of three or more syllables (go'gome) against Tauberschmidt's initial stress on Saroa trisyllables; this is a different dialect in a one-sentence sketch remark and does not outrank

tone.quote: 5.0 Supra-segmental Items 5.1 Stress and Pitch on Words On one to three syllable words stress and high pitch is on the first syllable. (Hyphen indicates morpheme breaks). [`bai] ‘pig’ [`nu.ma] ‘house’ [`vo.vo.ka] ‘plenty’ [`ai.ʝe.si] ‘how are you’ On words with four syllables the first and penultimate syllable is stressed. The stress on the first syllable is stronger though. [`ɤa.li.`va.ta] ‘banana’ ... 5.2 Stress and Pitch on Words in a Phrase Stress and high pitch of an isolated word can change when it occurs in a phrase. [`ka.ra -da.`ga.ra?] ‘what thing?’ The stress of the second word is on the second syllable and high pitch is on the first.
tone.locator: sec. 5.0 'Supra-segmental Items', 5.1 'Stress and Pitch on Words' and 5.2 'Stress and Pitch on Words in a Phrase' (p.16)
tone.summary: No tone system described: high pitch is a positional correlate of fixed word-initial stress (plus phrase-level shifts and question intonation); phoneme inventory has no tonemes.
